opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I've lived inside that culture for a while, and I have mixed feelings about it.

On one hand, the optimization mindset is a big part of why Silicon Valley works. People are very good at taking a goal, breaking it down, finding the metric, and grinding on it. If you know where you're going, that's incredibly powerful. You get speed, you get focus, and you don't waste energy on things that don't matter.

But there's a hidden assumption: that you already know which path is worth optimizing for. And very often, especially early in a career or early in a company, you don't. So what happens is people pick a lane very early. You go to the right school, you get the right internship, you join the right big tech company or the hot startup, and every step is "optimal" relative to that ladder. Then ten years later you look up and realize you've become extremely good at a game you never really chose. You just inherited it.

I see the same thing with companies. Everyone is chasing the same category at the same time, the same benchmark, the same kind of fundraising story. Locally it's rational, since that's where the capital and talent are. But collectively it means a lot of very smart people are crowded onto one narrow path, and the space of ideas that get explored shrinks.

What I've come to appreciate more is the value of what looks inefficient: wandering a bit, doing something that doesn't fit neatly on a résumé, spending time in a different field or a different country, talking to people outside your bubble. In the moment it feels like you're falling behind. But a lot of truly original work comes from people who have some strange combination of experiences that nobody would have designed on purpose. You can't optimize your way into that. You kind of have to stumble into it.

So my view is: optimize hard once you've found something you genuinely believe in, but be careful about committing too early. Keep some slack in the system. Leave room for exploration before you start exploiting, because the cost of climbing the wrong mountain very efficiently is actually really high.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that tendency comes from a real strength, which is that Silicon Valley is very good at finding the local optimum fast. You pick a wedge, you build the team around it, you iterate on metrics every week, and you squeeze out every bit of efficiency. For a lot of problems that works beautifully.

But I've become a bit skeptical of applying it everywhere, especially in a field like AI where the landscape itself is still shifting under your feet. When you optimize every step, you implicitly assume you already know which direction is up. If the terrain is going to change in six months, all that early optimization can actually lock you into a path that turns out to be a dead end. You've built a very efficient machine for climbing the wrong hill.

The companies I admire more tend to keep a certain looseness for longer than feels comfortable. They run several bets in parallel, they tolerate what looks like waste, and they delay the moment of commitment until the signal is genuinely clear. That looks inefficient from the outside, and investors sometimes hate it, but I think it's often the more rational strategy under high uncertainty.

So my view is roughly this: optimize hard once you know what game you're playing. Before that, the most valuable thing is keeping your options open and learning fast, not being efficient. The mistake is confusing those two phases, and I think the Valley culture pushes people into the second phase too early.

astra-6.text:
I think optimization is useful once you know what you’re optimizing for. The danger is that you commit to a path before you’ve really asked whether it’s yours. You can become very good at winning a competition you didn’t consciously choose.

And once every step has to contribute to that goal, there’s less room to wander, to try something you’re bad at, or to change your mind. Those things look inefficient, but they can help you discover what you actually care about.

So I wouldn’t say don’t commit. Commitment lets you do difficult things. I’d just leave some space to question the direction, even while you’re working hard at it. Am I still curious about this? Do I want the work itself, or do I mostly want the recognition that comes with succeeding at it?

sol-6.1.text:
I think optimization is useful once you know what you’re optimizing for. The danger is committing to that answer too early. You can get very good at moving along a path without asking whether it’s a path you actually want to be on.

And competition makes that harder, because it gives you such a clear measure of progress. You’re catching up, you’re getting ahead—but according to whose definition? I think you need some room to explore, to do things that don’t have an obvious payoff, and to change your mind. Otherwise, every step can look rational while the overall direction goes unquestioned.
